opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot. People often assume the hard part is the hardware, getting a robot hand with enough degrees of freedom and good enough actuation. That matters, but I don't think it's the main bottleneck anymore. The harder problem is the gap between what a human hand does and what we can actually capture and transfer.

There are a few pieces. First, sensing and data. When you watch a person manipulate something, say rotating a pen or opening a jar, most of what matters isn't visible. It's in the contact: where the fingertips touch, how much force, how the object slips and gets caught again. Video gives you kinematics at best, and even that is hard because fingers occlude each other and the object. So we need better ways to capture human manipulation, like gloves, wearable sensors, and tactile skins, that record not just where the hand is but how it's interacting with the world.

Second, embodiment mismatch. Even a very anthropomorphic robot hand differs from a human hand in finger lengths, joint limits, compliance, skin friction, and above all sensing. Our fingertips have incredibly dense tactile feedback. So you can't just copy the joint angles. Naive retargeting often gives you something that looks right but fails physically, because the contacts aren't where they need to be. I think the right level of transfer is more about intent and contact: what the human is trying to do to the object, which surfaces they're using, which forces they're applying. Then the robot works out how to achieve that with its own body.

Third, I think the human data gives you the prior, and the robot has to close the loop itself. Human demonstrations can tell you which strategies are worth trying, how to approach an object, what a reasonable grasp looks like. But the fine-grained, closed-loop part of dexterity, constantly correcting based on touch, probably has to be learned or refined on the robot, through its own interaction, in simulation, the real world, or both. So I see it as a combination: learn the structure of the behavior from people at scale, then adapt it to the robot's own embodiment through practice.

And underneath all of that is scale. Language models took off partly because there was an internet's worth of text. For dexterous manipulation we don't have that yet. But humans use their hands constantly, all day, everywhere. If we can capture even a fraction of that in a form that's useful for robots, I think that's what unlocks real dexterity. So for me, the key question isn't only how to build a better hand. It's how to turn everyday human hand activity into a scalable source of robot learning.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a substantial transfer gap involving missing contact data and embodiment mismatch, rather than expressing that the gap is relatively small.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose an integrated hand-and-arm actuator stack or compare transfer to UMI gripper transfer; it emphasizes data capture and robot practice instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So that's a question I think about a lot, because on paper it sounds like it should be straightforward: humans have five fingers, you build a robot hand with five fingers, you record what the human does, and you replay it. In practice, almost every step of that breaks down, and I think it's worth being honest about where.

The first problem is the data itself. If I want to learn from human hand behavior, I need to observe it at a level of detail that actually matters for manipulation. And most of what makes a grasp work is not the big motion of the fingers. It's the contact: where the fingertips land, how much force each one applies, how the object shifts as you squeeze it. Vision gets you the coarse pose reasonably well these days, but it's bad at exactly the things that matter most. Fingers occlude each other, the object occludes the fingers, and you basically never see forces. So you can collect hours of video of people doing things with their hands and still be missing the signal you need.

The second problem is embodiment. Even a very good five-finger robot hand is not a human hand. The kinematics are different, the joint limits are different, the tendons or motors behave differently, the skin is different, the compliance is different. So "retargeting" a human pose to a robot pose is not a lookup table. If you naively map joint angles, the robot fingertips end up in slightly the wrong places, and in manipulation slightly wrong is the same as wrong. You drop the object. What you really want to preserve is the functional structure of the behavior, the contact relationships between hand and object, rather than the literal joint trajectory. That's a much more interesting optimization problem, and I don't think we've fully solved it.

The third problem, and I think this is the one people underestimate, is that human demonstrations are not sufficient on their own. A human doing a task one time shows you one successful path. It doesn't show you what to do when the object slips or when it's rotated ten degrees from where it was in the demo. Dexterous manipulation is a contact-rich, high-dimensional control problem, and the space of ways it can go wrong is enormous. So I think human data is best thought of as a prior. It tells the robot roughly what strategies look like, which fingers to use, what the sequence of contacts should be. Then you need something on top of that, whether it's reinforcement learning, or large-scale simulation, or real-world practice with correction, to make the behavior actually robust on the robot's own body.

So if I had to summarize what it would take, I'd say three things. Better ways to capture human hands that get at contact and force, not just pose. Retargeting methods that preserve what the hand is doing to the object rather than what the joints are doing in space. And a learning pipeline that treats the human demonstration as a starting point, not as the answer. The encouraging part is that all three of those are moving quickly. The hardware is getting better, simulation is getting much more realistic, and we have far more human video than we used to. I don't think we're at the point where you can just show a robot hand something and have it work. But I think the gap between what humans do and what robot hands can do is closing faster now than it has at any point in my career.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer is not yet straightforward and describes substantial data, embodiment, and robustness challenges. Saying the gap is closing does not communicate that it is relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose an integrated dexterous-hand-and-arm actuator stack or compare transfer to UMI gripper transfer.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that transferring the motion is only part of the problem. A human hand and a robot hand can both have five fingers, but their joint limits, proportions, and strength can be quite different. So you don’t necessarily want the robot to copy every joint angle. You want it to achieve the same interaction with the object.

For example, if I’m picking up a cup, what matters is where I make contact, whether the grasp is stable, and how much force I apply. Watching my hand can give the robot a useful starting point, but it doesn’t directly tell you all of those forces. That’s where tactile sensing and feedback become really important: can the robot detect that the cup is slipping and adjust its grip?

So I’d approach it as a combination of learning from human demonstrations and practicing with the robot’s own body. Human behavior gives you a strong prior for what to do, and robot experience teaches you how to actually do it with that particular hardware. The challenge is making that process work across lots of objects and situations, rather than just reproducing one successful demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response describes differences in hand hardware and the need for robot-specific practice; it does not say the human-to-robot transfer gap is relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose an integrated hand-and-arm actuator stack or compare transfer to UMI gripper transfer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that transferring the motion of five fingers isn’t quite the same as transferring the skill. A human hand and a robot hand have different geometry, different joint limits, and different ways of making contact. So if I demonstrate picking up a cup, the goal shouldn’t necessarily be for the robot to reproduce every joint angle. It should reproduce the important interactions: where to make contact, how to support the cup, and how to keep it stable as it moves.

That means we need a way to capture human demonstrations, map them onto what the robot can actually do, and then let the robot learn through interaction. Vision helps, but touch and force feedback become really important. When something starts slipping, you adjust your grip almost without thinking. A robot needs that kind of feedback loop, too.

So I would think of human behavior as a starting point, rather than a complete control program. The harder part is giving the robot enough experience to adapt that behavior to its own hand and to objects and situations it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The candidate emphasizes differences in hand geometry, joint limits, and contact, but does not say the transfer gap is relatively small.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses capturing demonstrations, mapping them to the robot, and learning through interaction, but does not propose an integrated hand-and-arm actuator stack or compare transfer to UMI gripper transfer.
